🚀 We're Hiring: Video Caption Auditor Expert
💰 Pay: $20–$30/hour
🌎 Location: Remote (Worldwide)
💼 Type: Hourly Contract
🏢 Company: Mercor
📩 Apply now: https://t.mercor.com/2epIN

🚀 Role Overview
Mercor is looking for detail-oriented annotators to review captions on egocentric (first-person) videos. These videos are recorded using head-mounted cameras and show people performing everyday activities such as cooking, cleaning, and crafting.
Your task will be to watch short video segments, check whether the written captions accurately describe the visible actions, and provide a clear verdict.
📋 Key Responsibilities
✅ Review short first-person video segments alongside their captions
✅ Approve captions that accurately describe the visible actions
✅ Reject incorrect captions and classify errors as Major or Minor
✅ Identify incorrect main actions, missing or added actions, and actions shown in the wrong order
✅ Check object names, tools, and left/right hand references
✅ Exclude unusable footage, including corrupted videos or incorrectly mounted cameras
✅ Follow detailed guidelines and apply evaluation criteria consistently
✅ Judge only what is visibly happening in each video segment
🎯 Ideal Candidate Profile
✅ Excellent attention to detail and patience for repetitive visual review
✅ Strong English reading comprehension
✅ Ability to understand precise differences between action words such as "wipe," "rub," and "scrub"
✅ Reliable left/right reasoning from the camera wearer's point of view
✅ Ability to quickly learn and follow detailed project guidelines
✅ Good judgment when handling ambiguous cases
⭐ Nice to Have
✅ Previous experience in video annotation or data labelling
✅ Experience in content moderation or quality assurance
✅ Background in AI training, annotation, or evaluation projects
📌 Project Details
• Short-term, fast-moving project
• Project is already underway, with priority given to candidates who can start quickly
• Fully remote opportunity – work from anywhere
• Flexible working schedule
• Detailed guidelines and practical examples provided
• Quick onboarding process
• Strong performance may lead to future AI training and evaluation opportunities
• Independent contractor engagement
• Weekly payments through Stripe or Wise
• Projects may be extended, shortened, or concluded early depending on business needs and performance
• H1-B and STEM OPT candidates are not supported at this time
🌟 Why Join Mercor?
Contribute to cutting-edge AI development by helping advanced models understand and interpret real-world human actions through video. Apply your observation skills, language understanding, and attention to detail while working on meaningful AI evaluation projects.
📩 Apply now: https://t.mercor.com/2epIN

AI Agents Need Job Descriptions, Not Just Prompts

A prompt tells an AI what to do. A job description tells it what it is allowed to do, what it must never do, and who answers when something goes wrong.

The question nobody is asking?
Imagine hiring a new employee tomorrow. You give them access to your email, customer database, financial systems, cloud storage, code repository, and payment tools. Then you say: “Be helpful. Figure out the rest.”

No sensible organization would do that.
Yet that is increasingly how companies are deploying AI agents: powerful systems are connected to business tools and given broad permissions, while their purpose, limits, and accountability remain vague. The result is not a digital employee. It is an unsupervised insider with excellent language skills.

That shift from “answering questions” to “doing work” is why they need the same discipline we apply to human hiring.

Adoption is racing ahead?
The issue is whether companies are deploying them like responsible professionals or like magical black boxes with administrator access.

A prompt is not a contract
A prompt is temporary instruction. 
A job description is a durable operating agreement

The second version creates boundaries. The first creates risk.
A useful AI-agent job description should answer five questions:
1.	What is your role?
2.	What data can you access? Only the minimum data required for the task.
3.	What actions can you take? Read, draft, recommend, execute, or approve?
4.	When must you stop? High-risk actions should require human approval.
5.	Who is accountable? A named human owner, not the model.

Autonomy needs guardrails?
The most important principle is simple: an AI agent should have the least access necessary to do its job.
NIST guidance emphasizes least privilege, tightly scoped authorizations, continuous verification, and clear escalation paths when risk thresholds are reached.
This is not bureaucracy. It is basic operational hygiene.

The accountability gap
When an AI agent makes a mistake, “the AI did it” is not an acceptable answer
A strong governance model separates responsibilities:
•	Owner: Decides what the agent is for and approves its deployment.
•	Security team: Controls identity, access, logging, and monitoring.
•	Business user: Reviews outputs and handles exceptions.
•	Risk or compliance team: Defines prohibited actions and escalation rules.
•	The agent: Executes only within its defined scope.
AI can assist decisions, but it should not become the place where responsibility disappears.

In summary, An AI agent without a job description is an unmanaged risk with a polished interface. 
The Orgs that win will be those that give it the clearest purpose, the narrowest permissions, and the strongest human accountability.
AI agents do not need to be treated like humans. But they absolutely need to be managed like employees: with a role, limits, supervision, and consequences.

Qantas is cutting 850 jobs in Australia and outsourcing corporate functions to Accenture, with much of the work moving to India.
AI and technology transformation are among the reasons cited. There is an interesting contradiction here.

For years, companies outsourced work to India because labour was cheaper.
Now AI is supposed to reduce the need for labour itself.
Yet one of the world's major airlines is moving hundreds of roles to an IT services company, largely in India, while preparing for an AI-driven future.

Perhaps we are still in the transition phase.

First, work moves from expensive employees to lower-cost service providers.
Then AI and automation reduce the people needed to deliver that work.

For Indian IT services companies, this creates both an opportunity and a threat.
We may win more outsourcing contracts in the short term while gradually reducing the human effort required to service them.

And that challenges the traditional IT services model, where revenue growth has often meant hiring more people.

The next generation of IT services companies may be judged less by how many people they employ and more by how much work they deliver without adding people.

I did two AI-led interviews recently. They couldn’t have been more different.
  
Interview 1: about 90% human-like, with instant voice replies and a natural flow. The one flaw: if I paused for 5 seconds to think, it assumed I was done and moved on to the next question.
  
Interview 2: a robotic voice and a stiff, unnatural flow. Honestly, it was annoying.
  
Then the second company sent the contract. The fee was lower than advertised, and lower than the industry average. I turned it down without regret.
  
What I learned:
  1.     An AI-led interview is only as good as the planning and implementation behind it. Small design choices, like how long it waits during a pause, change who gets a fair chance.
  2.     AI can take over parts of the process, but oversight, evaluation, and final decisions must stay with humans.
  3.     In any AI workflow, the model’s power is only part of the story. Planning, implementation, review, and continuous improvement matter just as much.
  4.     Never accept an offer that doesn’t reflect your experience and value, however smooth the process was.
  
Have you done an AI-led interview? How did it go?

Ras Malé Waterfront | A master-plan tender is a planning step

12 November 2026 · Eagle Hills analysis

A government Gazette notice dated 10 November invites proposals to prepare the Ras Malé master plan. It sets 16 November at 12:00 for clarification questions and 2 December at 09:00 for bid submission. Those are different deadlines.

The notice is evidence of a planning procurement process. It does not announce a consultant appointment, a completed master plan or a final development agreement with Eagle Hills.

Eagle Hills’ own announcement of 21 September describes signed commercial terms, with detailed terms still to be developed. As of this morning, our source checks found no public confirmation of a signed final agreement. Parliament’s record still lists the Real Estate Development Bill at first reading.

Why does the wider plan matter to the proposed waterfront and marina? A district needs to fit into the surrounding city: housing, transport, utilities, public spaces and coastal protection cannot be assessed only inside a developer’s boundary.

Analysis: the Maldives could gain jobs, homes, orders for local suppliers, public revenue and US dollar inflows. The value retained locally would depend on hiring, purchasing and payment arrangements. Imported materials and overseas services would also use foreign currency. Infrastructure costs and impacts on reefs, water quality and coastal conditions need to be assessed alongside the benefits.

For Eagle Hills, a coherent wider plan could reduce uncertainty around access and services, supporting property sales, development returns and its regional brand. These are potential gains for a UAE-based private company; they do not establish a return to the UAE government.

Planning documents and final contracts should show which facilities are funded, who pays, when homes and public benefits arrive, and how environmental performance will be monitored. Estimated development value describes an intended scale. It is not proof of committed financing, guaranteed sales or guaranteed state revenue.

Getting a Japanese Corporate VC on your cap table is like getting married on the first date:

Lots of celebration, huge commitment, but suddenly you need 14 approvals just to change the color of your robot. 🇯🇵🤝🤖

In Japan’s Deep Tech ecosystem, CVCs are everywhere. 

While traditional VC funds hesitate to write checks for heavy hardware, climate-tech, and Physical AI, corporate giants (from automakers to electronics leaders) step in with deep pockets and world-class labs.

Sounds like a founder's dream, right? 

Well, welcome to the "CVC Paradox":

1️⃣ The Infinite PoC Loop 🔄
You pitched a 6-month pilot to integrate your AI vision model into their factory. 18 months later: You are on PoC Version 4.2, spent $200k on custom integration, and haven't signed a single commercial contract.

2️⃣ "Strategic Alignment" vs. Speed 🐢
Pure VCs care about valuation and your next Series B. 
CVCs care about strategic synergy with a parent division. If the internal corporate champion who backed your startup gets rotated to another department (a classic Japanese HR move), your project freezes.

3️⃣ The Exclusivity Trap 🪤
A Japanese CVC gives you money, but hints that you shouldn't sell your dual-use sensors to their competitors. Congratulations, your global market size just shrank by 70%.

DON'T GET ME WRONG: Japanese CVCs bring unmatched infrastructure, trusted supply chains, and real manufacturing depth. 

The secret to surviving CVC backing isn't avoiding them—it’s operational discipline.

Founders need to treat corporate partnerships not as "cool R&D experiments," but as strict, deadline-driven delivery projects with clear milestones, metrics, and commercial exit ramps from PoC purgatory.

Brilliant technology gets you the CVC check. 
Disciplined project management gets you the actual contract.

How do you keep corporate pilots from dragging on forever? 👇

• Week 2: Prove It with a Clickable Prototype. We build a working, interactive prototype you can actually click through on your screen. The plan is the product; the prototype is the proof. It lets you feel the workflow and validate it before you commit major capital.

• Week 3: The Build-Ready Plan & Cost Estimate. You leave with a complete technical specification, recommended tech stack, phased rollout plan (MVP vs. Phase 2), and a grounded cost estimate for the full build—so you know what to budget before hiring a dev team.

Best of all: we don't lock you in. The roadmap and prototype are yours to take to any developer, and if you choose to build with NRTech, your entire Sprint fee is credited toward your development contract.

If an algorithm screens out a Colorado applicant on January 2, could you explain why within 30 days?

Colorado’s automated decision-making law (SB 26-189) takes effect January 1, 2027. It replaced the broader Colorado AI Act this spring and reaches employers whose automated tools materially influence hiring, promotion, discipline or termination decisions about Colorado applicants and employees.

  • Notice before the tool is used.
  • A plain-language explanation within 30 days after an adverse outcome, including the tool’s role and the personal data it relied on.
  • A way to correct inaccurate data, plus meaningful human review where commercially reasonable.
  • Records kept for 3 years.

AI isn't taking jobs in the future.

It's taking them now.

Between Jan - Sep 2026, US companies cited AI for 120,136 job cuts — 21% of all cuts. Up from 54,836 in all of 2025.

And the worst hit? Not seniors.

Workers aged 22-25 in AI-exposed roles saw employment fall 19%. Companies aren't just firing. They're not hiring juniors at all.

But some countries are fighting back. And their playbooks are very different:

🇨🇳 China: Prevent before it happens
18-point plan. Companies must do an employment-risk assessment BEFORE deploying AI at scale. Plus an "unemployment buffer period" — advance notice + retraining + internal transfer.

🇮🇹 Italy / EU: A human must decide
From Oct 2026, Italy made it law: No firing, hiring, or discipline decision can be made by AI alone. If it is, it's void. Fines up to €35M.

🇰🇷 South Korea: Make companies pay
Proposed world's first "AI Transition Levy" — if AI causes major layoffs, you pay into a fund for retraining and income support. Keep headcount, pay less.

🇺🇸 US: Still patchwork
No federal law. Only WARN notice (60 days), state rules, and union contracts. New York asked companies to report if AI caused layoffs. In 1 year, 0 companies said yes.

The lesson is clear:

We can't stop AI.
But we CAN decide who pays for the transition.

No fully automated firing.
Advance notice, not a sudden pink slip.
Share the productivity gains.

If you're in customer support, junior dev, content, data, or back-office — don't compete WITH AI.

Learn to work WITH it. That's your real job security now.

What do you think — should your country tax AI layoffs like South Korea, or ban automated firing like Italy?

Most finance professionals have NO IDEA what's actually inside a Claude Plugin.

And understanding these 4 building blocks could completely change how you use AI at work.

👉 Want to unlock Claude's full potential for finance? I'll show you how to use these tools in my free AI CFO Masterclass, live every Tuesday: https://lnkd.in/gHXDw7rV

Think of a Claude Plugin as hiring a specialist who arrives with their own playbook, tools, and instructions.

Instead of setting everything up from scratch, you get a package designed for specific tasks.

Here's what's actually inside 👇

1. Skills: Your Playbook

Skills are reusable instructions that tell Claude HOW to complete a task.

For example:

- Analyze budget vs actual variances
- Prepare financial reports
- Follow reconciliation checklists
- Create standardized management commentary

Claude can automatically load the relevant skill when your task matches.

2. Slash Commands: Your Shortcuts

Instead of writing the same long prompt repeatedly, type "/" to access available commands.

Think of them as shortcuts for workflows you use regularly.

3. Connectors: Your Data Access

Connectors let Claude access external tools and data sources.

Depending on the plugin, these can include:

- BigQuery for financial data
- Slack for team information
- Notion for documentation
- Box for stored files
- Asana for project management

But installing a plugin doesn't automatically connect your accounts.

You still need to configure and authorize each connector.

4. Agents: Your Specialists

In supported Claude environments, agents can handle specific parts of larger tasks.

For example, different specialists could support research, analysis, or documentation.

The four plugins shown don't use agents, but it's another capability worth understanding.

Here's something important.

You don't need to connect every tool to start using Claude Plugins.

You can upload your Excel files, ERP exports, or other documents directly.

And if your company uses an ERP system, you can connect a compatible MCP server or work with exported data.

My recommendation?

Start with one plugin relevant to your work.

Finance for reporting and reconciliation.

Data for cleaning, analysis, and dashboards.

Operations for processes and compliance.

Legal for contracts and reviews.

Pick one repetitive task, test the workflow, and verify the results before using them.

That's how you turn Claude from a chatbot into a practical tool for your finance team.
